title: Recall Quiz: Phonemes, Syllables, Stress & Intonation

options: Two words differing by one phoneme
questions.explanation: A minimal pair differs by exactly one sound, like 'cat' and 'bat'.

questions.q: What is the mandatory part of a syllable?
questions.explanation: The nucleus (usually a vowel) is the essential core of a syllable.

questions.q: In the noun 'record', which syllable is stressed?
questions.explanation: Nouns typically have first-syllable stress (RE-cord), while verbs have second (re-CORD).

questions.q: Which intonation pattern is commonly used for Yes/No questions?
questions.explanation: Yes/No questions typically end with a rising intonation.

questions.q: Different variations of the same phoneme are called:
questions.explanation: Allophones are phonetic variations of a single phoneme that do not change meaning.

questions.q: A syllable ending in a consonant is called a:
questions.explanation: Closed syllables end with a coda (a consonant).

questions.q: What do we call the stress pattern where a word has an alternating rhythm of stressed and unstressed syllables?
questions.explanation: Iambic meter consists of unstressed followed by stressed syllables.

questions.q: Wh-questions typically use which intonation pattern?
questions.explanation: Information questions (Wh-questions) usually have a falling intonation.

questions.q: How many vowel phonemes are in Standard English?
questions.explanation: There are 20 vowel phonemes (12 monophthongs and 8 diphthongs).

questions.q: In the word 'strength', what is the syllable structure?
questions.explanation: 'strength' is /strɛŋθ/ -> CCC V CC (Wait, ngth is /ŋθ/ which is CC. So CCCVCC. Actually, let's use a simpler one.)
